A scientist noticed that South America and Africa look like puzzle pieces. Everyone laughed at him for fifty years. He was right — but for a reason he never figured out.

1. Read **The Man Who Was Laughed At** and watch how EVIDENCE piles up.
2. Learn the terms in the **Glossary**, then win the **Word Scramble** and the **Matching** game.
3. Follow **How We Figured It Out** — the timeline of the argument.
4. Sort the evidence in **What Kind of Boundary?**
5. Take the quiz — two questions ask what counts as EVIDENCE, not just what happened.
6. Fill in the **Cornell Notes** in your own words.
7. Lock the ideas in with **Remember the Earth Puzzle** — study the example aid, then make one your own.
8. Finish with **Explore: Reading a Coastline Like Wegener** — use what you learned on a real problem, and mark every guess as a guess.
9. Keep the **Three Ways Plates Meet** chart open while you sort — the three boundary types are the whole sort.

The real lesson here is not about rocks. It is about how science changes its mind when the evidence finally forces it. 🌍

from:
## The Man Who Was Laughed At

In 1912, a German scientist named Alfred Wegener pointed at a world map and said something that got him mocked for the rest of his life: the continents used to be joined together, and they have been drifting apart ever since.

His evidence was actually good. South America's east coast fits into Africa's west coast like puzzle pieces. Identical fossils of *Mesosaurus* show up on both continents. That reptile lived in fresh water and could never have swum an ocean. Matching rock layers and mountain ranges line up across the Atlantic. Coal sits under the ice of Antarctica, and coal forms in warm swamps. So Antarctica was not always where it is now.

Geologists still rejected it, and their reason was fair: Wegener could not explain **how**. What force could shove a continent through solid ocean floor? Without a mechanism, a good pattern is only a curiosity.

The answer arrived decades later, from the sea floor. After World War II, ships mapped the ocean bottom. They found a mountain range running down the middle of the Atlantic. Along that ridge, new rock was erupting and pushing outward. Even better, magnetic stripes frozen into that rock matched in mirror image on both sides. The sea floor was spreading.

Continents were not plowing through the ocean floor. They were riding on it.

Earth's outer shell is broken into about fifteen major **plates**. They float on the **mantle**, the hot layer of slowly flowing rock underneath.

Where plates pull apart at a **divergent** boundary, magma rises and makes new crust. That is Iceland, sitting on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and widening every year.

Where plates push together at a **convergent** boundary, one dives under the other or both crumple upward. That is the Himalayas, still growing as India presses into Asia.

Where plates grind past each other at a **transform** boundary, they stick, build stress, and snap. That is the San Andreas Fault. That snap is an earthquake.

Plates move about as fast as your fingernails grow, a few centimeters a year. Over millions of years, that is enough to build the Andes and tear open an ocean.

Wegener died on an expedition in Greenland in 1930, still dismissed. About thirty years later his idea became the foundation of modern geology.

Being right early is not the same as being believed. In science, you also have to show the mechanism.

## Following the Evidence

In 1912, Alfred Wegener proposed that continents had once been joined and later moved apart. He assembled several kinds of evidence. Some scientists supported continental drift; many objected, especially to his proposed forces and the idea of continents pushing through oceanic rock.

The Atlantic margins of South America and Africa have complementary shapes. Their submerged continental margins fit better than modern shorelines, which erosion and sea-level change can alter. Related fossils, matching rock sequences and mountain belts also occur across the Atlantic. The distribution of Mesosaurus, an aquatic reptile, was more readily explained by connected land than by crossing a wide ocean. Antarctic coal records former vegetation and very different environmental conditions. Coal alone does not prove continental movement; climate can change too. The strength is in several independent lines of evidence agreeing.

New ocean-floor evidence helped transform the debate in the mid-twentieth century. Mapping revealed ridge systems in detail. Oceanic rocks tend to get older away from spreading ridges, and bands recording past magnetic polarity often mirror one another on opposite sides. Together with earthquake patterns and other measurements, these findings supported seafloor spreading and the broader theory of plate tectonics.

A tectonic plate is a slab of lithosphere: crust plus rigid uppermost mantle. Plates can carry both continents and ocean floor. They move over warmer, mostly solid mantle that deforms slowly over long times. They do not float on a global ocean of liquid magma. Gravity acting on sinking slabs and elevated lithosphere, together with mantle motion, contributes to plate movement; the balance varies.

At divergent boundaries, plates move apart. Along ocean ridges, rising mantle partly melts and magma forms new oceanic crust. Iceland lies on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, and the East African Rift shows continental extension.

At convergent boundaries, plates move toward one another. Dense oceanic lithosphere can descend beneath another plate at a subduction zone, producing a trench and often a volcanic belt. The Andes are an example. Where continental lithosphere collides, crust can shorten and thicken, helping build mountains such as the Himalayas.

At transform boundaries, plates slide past. Locked fault patches store elastic stress and may suddenly slip, producing earthquakes. Other patches creep. Earthquakes also occur at other boundaries and within plates.

Rates vary, but a few centimeters per year is common. Small annual movements become large changes over millions of years. Wegener died in 1930, decades before plate tectonics became widely accepted in the 1960s. His proposal was an important precursor, not the complete modern theory. Science can recognize strong evidence before every mechanism is known; new tests help distinguish competing explanations.

from: It tells us Antarctica was once in a warm, swampy climate, so it must have been located somewhere very different. It counts as evidence because coal cannot form in polar ice conditions, so the continent itself must have moved.
to: Coal supports past vegetation and environmental conditions different from today. Climate can change without plate motion, so coal alone does not prove drift. Combine it with independent fossil, rock and seafloor evidence.

from: They required a mechanism — an explanation of what force could move continents — not just matching patterns. Reasonable answers can argue either way: the standard protected science from accepting coincidences, but it also delayed a correct idea for fifty years.
to: Seafloor ages, magnetic bands and earthquake patterns supported spreading, subduction and moving lithospheric plates. This differed from continents plowing through ocean floor. Strong evidence can matter before a mechanism is fully known; scientists still compare alternatives and test explanations.

from: Probably. Geologists model a future supercontinent forming in about 250 million years. It already has proposed names, like Pangaea Proxima. Nobody will be around to check.
to: Another supercontinent may form over hundreds of millions of years. Several scenarios are modeled, but its shape, timing and location are uncertain.

from: The horseshoe of volcanoes and earthquake zones around the Pacific. Plates converge there and dive under each other. About three-quarters of the world's active volcanoes sit along it.
to: The Pacific margin has many volcanoes and earthquake zones. Subduction accounts for many volcanic belts, but not every boundary around the Pacific is convergent.
